notes: Mortgage subrogation and possession appeal; four preliminary issues and Banque Financiere principles are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Mortgage subrogation and possession after BCCI refinancing
key_facts: C&G advanced £240,375 in July 1991 to refinance mortgages over the Appleyards' home, paying off Bradford & Bingley and paying BCCI on the day BCCI went into liquidation.
BCCI's liquidators refused to acknowledge receipt or consent to registration, leaving C&G with only an equitable charge while the BCCI charge remained registered.
C&G obtained suspended possession in 1992 proceedings based on the C&G mortgage but later pursued fresh proceedings claiming subrogation to B&B's redeemed first charge.
BCCI agreed in May 2002 not to dispute C&G's subrogation claim, and Judge McGonigal determined preliminary issues in C&G's favour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a trial of preliminary issues on whether C&G could obtain possession by equitable subrogation to a redeemed first mortgage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; C&G entitled to subrogation to B&B's rights and to possession, rejecting arguments on merger, perfection of security, Henderson abuse, and laches.
enrichment.ratio: Where a lender advances money to discharge a prior secured creditor but fails to obtain the bargained-for first legal charge because a second chargee blocks registration, equitable subrogation to the redeemed charge may still arise; obtaining an equitable charge does not merge with or defeat that claim, and failure to raise subrogation in earlier possession proceedings is not necessarily an abuse of process.
legal_issues: Whether C&G could claim subrogation after obtaining an equitable C&G mortgage
Whether registration and BCCI's May 2002 agreement perfected C&G's security and extinguished subrogation
Whether raising subrogation in fresh proceedings was Henderson abuse
Whether laches barred enforcement of subrogated rights
linked_authorities: Burston Finance Ltd v Speirway Ltd [1974] 1 WLR 1648
Banque Financiere de la Cite v Parc (Battersea) Ltd [1999] 1 AC 221
UCB Group Ltd v Hedworth [2003] EWCA Civ 1717

confidence.notes: Four issues, subrogation principles, and dismissal are clearly resolved. Some register-entry analysis is fact-specific.

notes: Special removal of old on-licence quashed on section 15 jurisdiction; obiter guidance on discretion and expert evidence.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of special removal of old on-licence to Gresham Hotel
key_facts: Ultimate Leisure sought special removal of an old on-licence from Mims Bar to the Gresham Hotel in Newcastle after a compulsory purchase order for regeneration.
Local residents, trade objectors, and Newcastle City Council opposed the removal because of noise impact on a neighbouring care home.
Licensing justices granted special removal on 1 December 2003, treating service of the CPO as sufficient to satisfy section 15(1) conditions.
Claimants challenged both jurisdiction and the justices' exercise of discretion on structural suitability, noise attenuation, and toilet facilities.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review with permission treated as substantive hearing of challenge to licensing justices' special removal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed and remitted to a differently constituted panel; jurisdiction under section 15(1) was not satisfied when the CPO was made because 'about to be' requires certainty and imminence.
enrichment.ratio: For special removal under section 15(1) of the Licensing Act 1964, the premises must be or be about to be pulled down or occupied for a public purpose in a sense connoting practical certainty and imminence; making a CPO that still required confirmation and inquiry was insufficient, and the justices erred in treating it as automatically triggering special removal jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether section 15(1) special removal conditions were satisfied
Meaning of 'about to be pulled down or occupied' under section 15(1)
Whether justices could refuse removal on structural unsuitability grounds including noise and toilets
Whether reasons adequately resolved conflicting expert evidence
linked_authorities: R v Windsor Licensing Justices ex p Hodes [1983] 1 WLR 685

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction holding and quashing order are explicit. Discretionary guidance on noise and toilets is obiter but detailed.

notes: Child support time limits and Article 6 challenge on permission application; procedural history complex but outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Child support appeal time limits and Article 6 fairness

statutes_considered.title: Child Support, Pensions and Social Security Act 2000

key_facts: Mr Denson's child support maintenance was reassessed upward after a 1998 departure direction finding his lifestyle inconsistent with declared income.
He appealed the departure direction unsuccessfully and later sought review of the revised assessment, but his application in 2001 was long out of time.
Transitional appeal regulations imposed a 13-month outer limit on late appeals against pre-June 1999 decisions.
He renewed an application for permission to appeal, arguing the time limits infringed Article 6 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from a Child Support Commissioner's dismissal of appeal from an appeal tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused and application dismissed; 13-month appeal limit did not impair the essence of Article 6 access to justice.
enrichment.ratio: Statutory time limits for child support appeals, including a 13-month cut-off under the 1999 Regulations, pursue legitimate aims of legal certainty and finality and are proportionate; a litigant in person who had already appealed and been told of appeal rights cannot reopen stale proceedings years later on human rights grounds.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Denson's 2001 review application was out of time
Effect of transitional provisions in the 1992 and 1999 appeal regulations
Whether appeal time limits violated Article 6 ECHR
Whether time runs from tribunal decision or later Court of Appeal refusal
index_terms: Child Support Appeals Tribunals Procedure Regulations 1992
Social Security and Child Support Regulations 1999
linked_authorities: R (Denson) v Child Support Agency [2002] 1 FCR 460

confidence.notes: Article 6 and time-limit conclusions are clear. Transitional regulatory history is intricate but not outcome-critical.

notes: Trade mark exhaustion and Part 24 summary judgment; ECJ reference deferred pending fuller trial.

enrichment.short_title: Glaxo HIV drugs parallel import and trade mark exhaustion
key_facts: Glaxo sold HIV and respiratory drugs from France to intermediaries said to be for African destinations, but Dowelhurst imported 16 consignments from Switzerland into the UK.
The drugs bore standard French packaging and EMEA approval numbers, and Glaxo sought Part 24 summary judgment for trade mark infringement.
A deputy judge granted partial summary judgment on one batch and a qualified injunction, but held 15 batches raised real defences on exhaustion.
German and Swedish courts had reached conflicting views on whether delivery to French buyers put the goods on the EEA market.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from Part 24 summary judgment in trade mark infringement proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Glaxo's appeal dismissed and defendants' cross-appeal allowed; all 16 consignments to go to trial with no ECJ reference at this stage.
enrichment.ratio: Whether goods have been put on the EEA market for exhaustion under Article 7 of Directive 89/104 is arguable where the proprietor delivers to purchasers in France despite an intention that goods go to Africa; seller's uncommunicated intention alone does not clearly exclude exhaustion, and implied consent from EMEA-marked packaging may also require trial.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'put on the market in the EEA' for trade mark exhaustion
Whether Glaxo exhausted rights by delivering goods to French freight forwarders
Whether EMEA licence numbers on packaging implied consent to EEA circulation
Appropriate form of injunction and personal liability of Mr Taylor
linked_authorities: Zino Davidoff SA v A&G Imports Ltd (Case C-414/99)
van Doren v Lifestyle Sports (Case C-244/00)
Microsoft Corp v Technology Enterprises [1999] EWCA Civ 1854

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on arguability and trial disposal is clear. Exhaustion law remains unsettled pending ECJ and foreign decisions.

notes: CFA regulation 3(1)(b) breach and Hollins v Russell all-or-nothing unenforceability; short second appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Unenforceable CFA for failure to specify postponement element
key_facts: Mr Spencer settled a personal injury claim for £30,000 plus costs, but detailed assessment turned on enforceability of his CFA.
The CFA specified a 75% success fee but did not in the agreement itself state how much related to postponement of payment of fees.
A separate risk assessment ticked 'deferment of costs until conclusion of case - 50%' without explaining whether that meant 50% of the success fee or profit costs.
Following Hollins v Russell, the county court judge held the material breach rendered the entire CFA unenforceable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal with assessor from county court decision on detailed assessment of costs under a CFA.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; court refused to read down section 58(1) to permit partial enforceability after material regulatory breach.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 58(1) of the Courts and Legal Services Act 1990 as applied in Hollins v Russell, a material breach of the Conditional Fee Agreements Regulations 2000 renders the whole CFA unenforceable; the court cannot adopt a purposive partial-enforcement construction to save recoverable success fees.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 3(1)(b) required specification of postponement element in the CFA itself
Whether the breach materially adversely affected client protection
Whether unenforceability under section 58(1) should be partial or total
Recoverability of a 25% success fee if 50% of 75% related to postponement
linked_authorities: R (Quintavalle) v Secretary of State for Health [2003] UKHL 13

confidence.notes: Regulatory breach, Hollins application, and dismissal follow directly from established Court of Appeal authority.

notes: BSE feed-ban MRN judicial review succeeded on procedural unfairness; lengthy factual dispute but clear ground of success.

enrichment.short_title: BSE movement restriction notice judicial review for Kent beef herd
key_facts: Trading standards officers found suspected mammalian protein in feed at the Banks' Flintstones Farm herd in September 2002 during a BSE feed-ban inspection.
DEFRA served and later maintained a Movement Restriction Notice preventing the 247-head beef herd from entering the human food chain.
The claimants disputed deliberate feeding, sought test results for months, and challenged DEFRA's March 2003 decision to maintain the MRN.
The MRN was revoked in August 2003 and replaced with passport stamping, but the claimants contended that review process was procedurally unfair.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of DEFRA's decision to maintain a TSE Movement Restriction Notice after earlier notice served on the herd.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded on procedural unfairness; quashing and mandatory orders unnecessary after revocation, with damages unavailable for lack of identified cause of action.
enrichment.ratio: Although Parliament prescribed no appeal or review procedure for an MRN, DEFRA was obliged to keep its justification under review fairly; elementary fairness required timely disclosure of the case against the farmer and test results so representations could be made, and that standard was not met.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of maintaining the Movement Restriction Notice
Procedural fairness of DEFRA's review process
Whether test results and analysis had to be disclosed to the farmer
Whether passport stamping 'not for human consumption' was legally authorised

confidence.notes: Procedural unfairness success is explicit. Merits of feeding allegations and passport-stamping power were not finally decided.

notes: Criminal legal aid refusal quashed where clerk wrongly assumed fine-only outcome for Bail Act offences.

enrichment.short_title: Legal representation order for failure to surrender to bail
area_of_law: Legal aid and access to justice
key_facts: Miss Evans, a 24-year-old drug addict with prior bail offences, applied for criminal legal aid before trial for two failure-to-surrender charges.
The magistrates' clerk refused funding on the basis the issues were simple, involved no witnesses, and conviction would likely attract only a fine.
Case law and the Consolidated Criminal Practice Direction indicated custodial and usually consecutive sentences for Bail Act breaches.
The justices upheld the clerk's advice when the application was renewed orally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of magistrates' court refusal of a legal representation order in pending bail offence proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Decisions of 14 October and 7 November 2003 quashed; matter remitted for reconsideration of legal aid with proceedings stayed pending outcome.
enrichment.ratio: In deciding whether grant of legal representation serves the interests of justice under Schedule 3 to the Access to Justice Act 1999, magistrates must properly consider the likelihood of loss of liberty; it was not reasonable to assume a fine-only outcome for repeated failure-to-surrender offences given appellate guidance favouring custodial consecutive sentences.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of legal aid was compatible with the interests of justice
Likely sentence for failure to surrender to bail
Proper weight to be given to clerk's advice on funding
Relevance of R v White & McKinnon and Practice Direction guidance
linked_authorities: R v Neve (1989) 8 Cr App R (S) 270
R v White & McKinnon [2002] EWCA Crim 2952

confidence.notes: Statutory test, sentencing guidance, and quashing order are straightforward on the reported facts.

notes: Non-party costs order against Nigerian lawyer funding vessel detention defence; appeal allowed on pure funder analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Non-party costs order against funder of unlawful vessel detention defence
key_facts: Gulf Azov succeeded against Chief Idisi and his companies for wrongful detention of a vessel and crew and for duress payments after a rig cargo dispute in Nigeria.
Mr Egbe, a Nigerian lawyer, funded critical representation and provided $350,000 and other sums enabling Idisi to purge contempt and continue the November 1999 Commercial Court hearing.
The deputy judge found Mr Egbe personally intervened in the litigation and ordered him to pay £421,847.89 in unrecovered costs as a non-party.
Mr Egbe denied paying legal fees and sought to adduce fresh evidence on appeal, which the Court of Appeal refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against non-party costs order under CPR 48.2(1)(a) following substantive shipping and contempt proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; exceptional non-party costs order set aside because funding and assistance to enable representation did not justify liability for the successful party's costs.
enrichment.ratio: An order for costs against a non-party under section 51 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 remains exceptional; providing or arranging funding to enable an impecunious litigant to comply with court orders and be represented, without bad faith or personal interest in the outcome, does not ordinarily expose a pure funder or assister to pay the opposing party's costs.
legal_issues: Whether a non-party costs order could be made against Mr Egbe
Distinction between pure funding and controlling or directing litigation
Whether funding to purge contempt and secure representation justified costs liability
Causation of later appeal, assessment, and contempt costs
linked_authorities: Aiden Shipping Co Ltd v Interbulk Ltd [1986] AC 695
Symphony Group Plc v Hodgson [1994] QB 179
Hamilton v Al Fayed (No 2) [2002] EWCA Civ 665
MCA Records Inc v Charly Records Ltd [2002] FSR 26

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on pure funding and allowance of appeal is detailed. Underlying fraud findings against Idisi are background only.

notes: Section 172 RTA identification notices; single offence holding and proof of chief officer authority explained.

enrichment.short_title: Section 172 driver identification notices and duplicity
key_facts: Meera Mohindra and Joanne Browne were convicted by magistrates of failing to identify the driver of a vehicle after section 172 notices following speed camera offences.
Mohindra's information charged her as a person other than the keeper, based on an inference drawn from her silence despite being the registered keeper.
Prosecution evidence consisted only of a postal clerk's statement of service without annexed notices showing chief officer authority.
The point on authority was raised only after the prosecution case closed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' convictions on section 172(3) Road Traffic Act 1988 offences, heard together.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals allowed; section 172(3) creates one offence, but convictions could not stand for lack of evidence that the requirement was made by or on behalf of the chief officer of police.
enrichment.ratio: Section 172(3) creates a single offence of failing to comply with a valid section 172(2) requirement, so duplicity does not require separate informations for keeper and non-keeper obligations; however the prosecution must prove the requirement was made by or on behalf of the chief officer, normally by producing the notice, and should be permitted to reopen if the point is raised before the close of evidence.
legal_issues: Whether section 172(3) creates one or two offences
Whether magistrates could infer the defendant was not the keeper from silence
What evidence proves a requirement was made by or on behalf of the chief officer
Whether failure to prove authority was a procedural or substantive defect
linked_authorities: Secretary of State for Environment Transport and the Regions v Holt (2002) RTR 309

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and evidential requirements are comprehensively reasoned with formal conclusions for future prosecutions.

notes: Brief Nepal asylum permission refusal; no point of law identified at any tier.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal permission refused as totally without merit
key_facts: The appellant sought permission to apply for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision refusing permission to appeal an adjudicator's determination.
Her application had been dismissed for failure to comply with an order of Master Gladwell and she sought reinstatement.
The adjudicator did not accept her account and found a risk of trial on return to Nepal insufficiently established.
She failed to attend an oral hearing before the High Court judge and requested adjournment on unreadable documents.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to reinstate and for permission to apply for judicial review of an IAT refusal of permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application to reinstate refused; no point of law identified to justify appeal to the Court of Appeal and case held totally without merit.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator disbelieves an asylum appellant's factual account and neither the Immigration Appeal Tribunal nor the High Court identifies a point of law, the Court of Appeal will not grant permission merely because credibility and risk on return were disputed.
legal_issues: Whether there was an arguable point of law for permission to appeal
Whether failure to comply with Master Gladwell's order should be excused
Risk of criminal trial on return to Nepal

confidence.notes: Outcome and lack of point of law are clear, but the judgment is very short with minimal legal analysis.
